layer1_summary.paragraph: The period from 1968 to 1976 represents a formative era in Iron Arrow's institutional identity, during which the organization deepened its ceremonial traditions, expanded its public presence, and navigated the evolving social landscape of the University of Miami. The Micco years were marked by deliberate efforts to strengthen the ritual foundation of Iron Arrow while broadening its visibility and community engagement across campus.
bullets: The formal ritual practices of Iron Arrow were refined and codified during this period, giving the organization a more structured ceremonial character that reinforced its Native American-inspired traditions.
The Iron Arrow Ball emerged as a signature social event, serving as a key occasion for members to celebrate the organization's values and connect with the broader University of Miami community.

Increasing visibility efforts during the Micco years helped Iron Arrow become a more recognized symbol of honor and achievement on campus, raising its profile among students, faculty, and administrators.

The University of Miami itself was undergoing significant growth and transformation during this era, providing both opportunities and challenges for Iron Arrow to assert its relevance within a changing institution.

The leadership of the Micco during this period played a central role in guiding Iron Arrow through a time of heightened social consciousness, ensuring the organization remained connected to its founding ideals while adapting to new expectations.

NOTE TO RESEARCHER

- The source text provided (pp. 91–95) does not match the requested subsections (The Ritual, The Ball, Increasing Visibility) from Section Five: 1968–1976 The Micco Years.
- Provided pages contain: (1) a personal history by Dr. Diana Lopez beginning in 1963 on the Medical School campus, and (2) the start of a profile of Dr. Henry King Stanford as third president and third Iron Arrow sponsor.
- Key facts incidentally present in the provided text that may be relevant to Iron Arrow history:
  - Dr. Henry King Stanford tapped into Iron Arrow on November 10, 1966, at "the old tapping tree"
  - Chief Barry Richard welcomed Stanford into membership
  - Stanford wore his Seminole jacket at Homecoming events, including dancing with the student Homecoming Queen
  - Stanford was instrumental in establishing the tribe's tapping mound and firebowl near the bookstore beneath a ficus tree
  - Stanford helped place Iron Arrow membership plaques alongside the statue of Dr. Ashe in the foyer of the Administration Building
  - Stanford promoted the James Hutchinson Fund (initiated by Eugene Cohen) to acquire 50 oil canvases preserving Seminole Indian beauty and culture
  - Several of these canvases hung in the Office of the President at time of writing
